claims.text: Periodic multilayer interfaces impede dislocation propagation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings.
The high configurational entropy of each layer suppresses atomic diffusion processes that facilitate creep.
The coatings initially have well-defined alternating layers and intact interfaces.
The selected elevated-temperature, constant-load regime promotes time-dependent plastic deformation.
Dislocation motion and diffusion are active under the proposed testing conditions.
Multilayer interfaces serve as barriers to dislocation movement.
The multilayer interfaces block dislocation motion and pile-up.
High configurational entropy within individual layers limits atomic mobility and diffusion needed for creep.
The combined interfacial barrier and reduced-diffusion effects reduce time-dependent plastic deformation.
Under identical high-temperature, constant-stress conditions, high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings will have a significantly lower creep rate than the proposed controls.
High-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings will exhibit reduced dislocation activity relative to the proposed controls.
The proposed behavior applies where dislocation motion and diffusion-driven creep are significant.
The proposed behavior ceases to be applicable above thresholds for phase instability or high-temperature degradation.

contradictions.description: The uncertainty field says that the interface-barrier and entropy-based diffusion mechanisms are supported by existing rationale, but no supporting evidence records are cited.
